items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which component must be added before PC-A and PC-B can communicate?

exhibit.content:
+--------------------+
              |     SW-ACCESS      |   Layer 2 switch
              +--+--------------+--+
                 |              |
             VLAN 10         VLAN 20
       192.168.10.0/24    192.168.20.0/24
             PC-A              PC-B

Both hosts are addressed correctly for their own VLAN and both switch
ports show connected. Neither host can reach the other. Nothing else is
attached to SW-ACCESS.

options.text: A device that routes between the VLANs, such as a router or Layer 3 switch.
A second Layer 2 switch, so that each VLAN has a dedicated switch of its own.
A wireless LAN controller to coordinate the two segments centrally.
A next-generation firewall to permit the traffic between the two VLANs.

items.explanation: A Layer 2 switch forwards only within a VLAN, and the two hosts sit in different VLANs and different subnets, so something operating at Layer 3 has to move traffic between them. Option B adds switching capacity, which was never the shortage, and would leave both VLANs just as isolated. Option C names a device that manages access points and plays no part in routing between wired segments. Option D would filter traffic that no device is currently routing at all, so permitting it changes nothing.

known exploit signatures, and any matching packet must be dropped before it

options.text: A Layer 3 switch placed in front of the server, filtering traffic with access lists.

An IPS inspecting the traffic inline, so it can drop matching packets.

Option A filters on addresses and ports, which carries no signature knowledge. Option B has the same limitation and sits at the wrong point besides. Option C protects the host after the packet has already arrived, which the requirement explicitly rules out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which subnet is this Mac attached to?

exhibit.content:
MacBook:~ user$ ifconfig en0
en0: flags=8863<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
        options=400<CHANNEL_IO>
        ether 3c:22:fb:1a:2b:3c
        inet6 fe80::1c2f:8a3b:4d5e:6f70%en0 prefixlen 64 secured scopeid 0xb
        inet 10.44.130.55 netmask 0xffffe000 broadcast 10.44.159.255
        nd6 options=201<PERFORMNUD,DAD>
        media: autoselect
        status: active

items.explanation: macOS prints the mask in hexadecimal, and 0xffffe000 expands to 255.255.224.0, a /19 whose blocks step by 32 in the third octet; 130 falls in the block beginning at 128, which the broadcast address of 10.44.159.255 confirms. Option A assumes a /24 and takes the host's own third octet as the network. Option B applies the classful /16 for the 10.0.0.0 range and ignores the mask entirely. Option D pairs the correct prefix length with an address that is not on a /19 boundary.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can this Linux host reach its own subnet but nothing outside it?

exhibit.content:
user@host:~$ ip addr show ens192
2: ens192: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 00:0c:29:ab:cd:ef brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 172.20.14.55/26 brd 172.20.14.63 scope global ens192
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever

user@host:~$ ip route
172.20.14.0/26 dev ens192 proto kernel scope link src 172.20.14.55 metric 100

The host reaches 172.20.14.60 by address without trouble, but every
address outside 172.20.14.0/26 times out.

options.text: The routing table holds no default route, so off-subnet traffic has nowhere to go.
The interface is administratively down and cannot forward beyond the link.
The /26 prefix is too small to permit traffic to leave the local segment.
No DNS server has been configured, so remote destinations cannot be resolved by name.

items.explanation: The routing table lists only the connected 172.20.14.0/26 entry, with no default via line, so the kernel has nowhere to send anything that does not match that prefix. Option B is contradicted by the interface state, which reads UP,LOWER_UP with an address bound. Option C invents a prefix length that blocks routing; a /26 routes off-subnet as readily as any other. Option D is ruled out because the failures happen when addressing destinations numerically, which never involves DNS.

3: ens160: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP group default qlen 1000

Option C is the figure for a /26, two bits out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why did installing AP-D degrade performance across this floor?

exhibit.content:
Site survey of the 2.4 GHz band on one floor

    AP        Channel    Neighbouring cells overlap this AP's coverage
    ------    -------    --------------------------------------------
    AP-A            1    AP-B, AP-D
    AP-B            6    AP-A, AP-C, AP-D
    AP-C           11    AP-B
    AP-D            3    AP-A, AP-B

Users nearest AP-D report slow throughput and frequent stalls, and the
three other cells were stable before AP-D was installed.

options.text: AP-D is too close to AP-C, and both are serving the edge of the same coverage area.
AP-D uses a channel already carried by AP-A, so the two cells are duplicating traffic.
AP-D is transmitting at a higher power than the other three access points.
AP-D sits on channel 3, which overlaps both channel 1 and channel 6.

items.explanation: In the 2.4 GHz band each channel is far wider than the spacing between channel numbers, so only channels five or more apart avoid overlapping, which is why 1, 6 and 11 are the standard plan. Channel 3 sits two away from 1 and three away from 6, so AP-D interferes with AP-A and AP-B at once, matching the overlap column exactly. Option A points at AP-C on channel 11, which is eight away from AP-D and does not overlap it. Option B treats channel 3 and channel 1 as the same channel. Option C invents a power difference the survey never records.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which access point should this client associate with for the most reliable connection?

exhibit.content:
Client-side survey taken from one desk

    AP        Channel    Signal (RSSI)    Noise floor    SNR
    ------    -------    -------------    -----------    ----
    AP-1            1        -62 dBm        -92 dBm      30 dB
    AP-2            6        -57 dBm        -61 dBm       4 dB
    AP-3           11        -71 dBm        -94 dBm      23 dB

All three advertise the same SSID and the client may associate with any
of them.

options.text: AP-1, because it combines a strong signal with a quiet noise floor.
AP-2, because it shows the strongest received signal of the three.
AP-3, because channel 11 is furthest from the other two cells.
Any of the three, because all advertise the same SSID and are equivalent.

items.explanation: What matters is how far the signal rises above the noise, not its absolute strength, and AP-1's 30 dB signal-to-noise ratio is the widest margin available. Option B picks the strongest raw RSSI, but AP-2 sits in a noise floor of -61 dBm, leaving only 4 dB of usable margin, which is the trap this item is built around. Option C picks on channel separation, which affects neighbouring cells rather than this client's own link quality, and AP-3's 23 dB is still below AP-1's. Option D treats a shared SSID as meaning the radio conditions are identical.

Option D assumes the scan duplicated a single AP, but a single radio reports one BSSID per network.

Option B describes equal-cost paths, which apply within one table rather than across two. Option C assumes one entry wins, but both tables are shown populated and both are live. Option D looks for a mask difference, and the two prefixes are identical.

-------------------------------------------

----    -----------       --------    -----

A frame arrives on Gi0/1 in VLAN 1, addressed to destination MAC

options.text: Discards it and returns an error to the sending station.
Holds it until an ARP request resolves the destination.

Floods it out every VLAN 1 port except Gi0/1.

items.explanation: The destination 00de.ad00.beef appears nowhere in the table, making this an unknown unicast, and a switch floods those out every port in the frame's VLAN except the one it arrived on, so Gi0/2, Gi0/3 and Gi0/4 all receive a copy. Option A describes a router returning an unreachable message, which a switch does not do. Option B confuses switching with ARP, a process the sending host runs before the frame is built. Option C would send the frame back where it came from, which flooding explicitly excludes to avoid returning traffic to its source.

-------------------------------------------

----    -----------       --------    -----

PC-A has just been plugged into Gi0/5, an access port in VLAN 1, and its
MAC address 00ee.4433.2211 appears nowhere in the table. PC-A immediately

options.text: Floods the frame and learns nothing until 00bb.1122.3344 replies.
Forwards the frame out Gi0/2 but records PC-A only once it replies.
Records PC-A against Gi0/5 and forwards the frame out Gi0/2 only.
Records PC-A against Gi0/5 and floods the frame to every VLAN 1 port.

items.explanation: Two independent things happen to one frame: the switch reads the source address and records 00ee.4433.2211 against the ingress port Gi0/5, then looks up the destination, finds 00bb.1122.3344 already listed on Gi0/2, and forwards there alone. Option A misses the learning, which happens on the first frame from any source rather than waiting for a reply. Option B makes learning depend on a reply, when the source address of this very frame is what teaches the switch. Option D adds a flood that is unnecessary because the destination is already known.

Multimode fibre, which spans the distance without single-mode optics.
Single-mode fibre, the only medium rated beyond 100 m.
Copper twisted pair with a repeater placed at the midpoint of the run.

items.explanation: The run is 340 m, which is beyond copper's 100 m limit but comfortably inside multimode's 550 m, and multimode optics cost less than single-mode, so it is the cheapest medium that actually reaches. Option A ignores distance entirely and considers only speed, which copper does support but cannot deliver over 340 m. Option C would work but pays for reach the campus does not need. Option D adds active equipment mid-duct, which introduces a powered device and a failure point where a passive fibre run needs neither.

A contractor ran copper twisted pair between the ground-floor comms

    ------------------------    ---------------------
    Copper twisted pair         100 m

    Single-mode fibre           10 km and beyond

The copper run needs a crossover cable rather than a straight-through one.
Autonegotiation is disabled, so the ports never agree on a speed.
The run is 45 m beyond the copper limit, so no reliable link forms.

items.explanation: Twisted pair is specified to 100 m, and this run is 145 m, so signal attenuation prevents a link establishing at all no matter what is fitted at the ends, which is exactly why swapping transceivers and leads changed nothing. Option A describes a VLAN mismatch, which leaves ports up while blocking traffic rather than keeping them down. Option B invokes cable pinout, which modern switches resolve automatically and which would not survive the swap testing already done. Option C describes a mismatch that the exhibit rules out by stating both ports are configured identically.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Both ports were hardcoded as shown during a maintenance window. What is the result on this link?

!

      speed 100
      duplex full
!
SW8  interface GigabitEthernet0/1
      speed 1000
      duplex full

The link comes up at 100Mb/s, since the lower of the two speeds wins.
The link comes up but suffers a duplex mismatch and late collisions.
The link comes up at 1000Mb/s once SW7 renegotiates to match SW8.

items.explanation: Speed must match for an Ethernet link to establish at all, so hardcoding 100 on one end and 1000 on the other leaves both ports down; unlike duplex, speed is not something the two ends can disagree about while still passing frames. Option B invents a lowest-common-speed rule that applies to autonegotiation, which both ports have now been taken out of. Option C describes the duplex mismatch signature, but both ends here specify full duplex and never get far enough to exchange frames. Option D expects renegotiation from a port that has been hardcoded.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the exchange with 10.1.1.201 begin carrying payload in its very first frame, while the exchange with 10.1.1.200 spends three frames before any data moves?

options.text: The 10.1.1.201 exchange had already completed its handshake before the capture began.
The switch prioritised the 10.1.1.201 traffic and forwarded its handshake unrecorded.
UDP is connectionless and sends payload at once, while TCP opens a session first.
The 10.1.1.200 exchange is retransmitting because its first two attempts were lost.

items.explanation: Frames 1 to 3 are the SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK that open a TCP connection, and only frame 4 carries a request; the UDP exchange has no such setup and puts 76 bytes of payload on the wire at once, because UDP keeps no connection state. Option A invents an earlier handshake that UDP would never have performed. Option B suggests the analyser missed frames, but both directions of the UDP exchange are present. Option D reads the three-frame opening as retransmission, though each frame carries a different flag rather than repeating one.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Segment 8815 never appears in the voice stream, and no frame recovers it. What does the capture show about how each transport handles the loss?

options.text: TCP retransmitted its own loss, while the UDP stream carried on without it.
Both transports recovered, but the UDP retransmission fell outside the captured window.
Neither transport recovered; frame 13 is a duplicate the analyser has mislabelled.
UDP recovered first because its smaller frames retransmit faster than TCP's.

items.explanation: Frame 12 acknowledges a gap and frame 13 is labelled a retransmission of the same sequence, so TCP detected the loss and resent it without the application being involved. The RTP sequence jumps from 8814 to 8816 with nothing resending 8815, because UDP offers no recovery and leaves the decision to the application, which for voice is to move on. Option B expects a UDP retransmission the protocol cannot perform. Option C dismisses a retransmission the capture states plainly. Option D reverses which transport recovers and invents a size-based advantage.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which service is the one best carried over UDP, and for what reason?

exhibit.content:
Three services are being moved onto a new link

    Service              Requirement
    -----------------    ----------------------------------------
    File synchronise     Every byte must arrive, order matters,
                         a pause of a second or two is acceptable
    Live voice call      A lost sample is better discarded than
                         delivered late; delay must stay minimal
    Database replica     Missing records are unacceptable and the
                         receiver must detect any gap

options.text: File synchronise, because bulk transfers benefit from the lower per-segment overhead.
Live voice call, because a late sample is worthless and retransmitting one adds delay.
Database replica, because the receiver detects gaps itself and needs no transport help.
All three, because UDP's smaller header improves throughput on any type of traffic.

items.explanation: Voice is the one requirement that prefers loss to delay: a sample that arrives after its playback moment is useless, so the retransmission TCP would perform actively hurts, which is why UDP suits it. Option A picks a service whose stated requirement is that every byte arrives in order, which is exactly what TCP provides. Option C describes a service that calls missing records unacceptable, so it needs guaranteed delivery rather than gap detection alone. Option D generalises a header saving into a universal rule and ignores every stated requirement.

PC2's address lies outside the private range and requires translation.
The /26 mask places the two hosts in different subnets.
Both hosts resolve to the same network address, so their addresses conflict.

That PC1 reaches .65 confirms its own subnet works. Option A is wrong because the broadcast of PC1's subnet is .127. Option B misapplies private addressing, since all of 192.168.0.0/16 is private. Option D describes an address conflict, which would need the two hosts to share one address.

items.explanation: Each segment needs the smallest subnet that still fits it: 500 hosts need a /23 giving 510, 200 need a /24 giving 254, 100 need a /25 giving 126, and 50 need a /26 giving 62. Placed in descending order from 172.16.8.0 those four tile the /22 exactly. Option A starts with a /24, which offers only 254 addresses and cannot hold 500 hosts. Option B opens with the entire /22, leaving nothing for the other three. Option C assigns a /24 at 172.16.11.0 that swallows the /26 placed at 172.16.11.128.

items.explanation: The 255.255.255.192 mask is a /26, so the interface sits in the block from 10.10.10.64 to 10.10.10.127; the last address is the broadcast and is unusable, leaving .65 through .126 for hosts. Option A is the highest usable host address, one below the broadcast. Option C sits comfortably inside the usable range. Option B is a /27 with only 30 usable addresses and cannot hold 60 hosts. Option D is a /28 with 14 usable and falls further short still. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which entry is the shortest valid form of the recorded address?

items.explanation: Leading zeros in a group are dropped and the single longest run of all-zero groups is replaced by a double colon, which here is the three groups before 0AB0, giving 2001:DB8::AB0:0:CD. Option A uses two double colons, which is invalid because the expansion would then be ambiguous. Option C loses a digit from 0AB0, turning it into AB and producing a different address entirely. Option D drops leading zeros correctly but never applies the double colon, so it is valid yet not the shortest form.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which global unicast address does GigabitEthernet0/0 build for itself?

options.text: 2001:DB8:ACAD:1:1A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFE:FF3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E
2001:DB8:ACAD:1:21A:2BFF:FE4D:5E3C

items.explanation: Modified EUI-64 splits the MAC in half, inserts FFFE between the two halves, and inverts the seventh bit of the first byte, turning 00 into 02; 001A2B and 3C4D5E therefore become 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E under the configured prefix. Option A skips the bit inversion and leaves the first byte as 00, which is the single commonest omission. Option B writes the inserted value as FEFF rather than FFFE. Option D transposes the final two groups of the interface identifier.

options.text: Link-local addresses are always reachable, but global addresses require DHCPv6.
The two global addresses sit in different /64 prefixes, so they need routing.
The global addresses lack an EUI-64 interface identifier and cannot be pinged.
Global addresses require ipv6 unicast-routing on both routers before any ping.

items.explanation: The fourth group differs, making the prefixes 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 and 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::/64, so the two globals are on separate subnets and would need a router between them. Link-local pings still work because FE80 addresses are scoped to the shared link and do not depend on the prefixes at all, which is exactly what makes the fault look intermittent. Option A invents a DHCPv6 dependency for statically configured addresses. Option C treats EUI-64 as mandatory, but a manually written identifier is fine. Option D would prevent transit routing, not a directly connected ping.

switchport mode dynamic auto, then switchport access vlan 30

items.explanation: Setting the mode to access fixes the port so it never negotiates a trunk, and the access vlan command places its untagged traffic in VLAN 30, which is exactly what a single server needs. items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. How does SW1 handle the traffic arriving from the two devices on Gi0/1?

!

!

An IP phone is cabled to Gi0/1, and a PC is cabled into the switch port
on the back of that phone.

options.text: Both devices send tagged frames, the PC in VLAN 10 and the phone in VLAN 20.
Both devices send untagged frames, and the switch places all of it in VLAN 10.
The PC sends untagged frames into VLAN 10; the phone tags its own for VLAN 20.
The port turns into a trunk and carries VLANs 10 and 20 tagged in both directions.

items.explanation: A port with both an access VLAN and a voice VLAN carries two kinds of traffic at once: whatever arrives untagged lands in the access VLAN, while the phone is told through CDP to tag its own traffic for the voice VLAN. Option A would require the PC to tag, which an ordinary host does not do. Option B ignores the voice VLAN entirely. Option D describes a trunk, and the configuration reads switchport mode access, which the voice VLAN does not change.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why can VLAN 20 hosts not reach their gateway while VLAN 10 hosts can?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - router on a stick
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 30
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
SW1 carries VLANs 10 and 20 across the trunk to R1. Hosts in VLAN 10
reach 192.168.10.1 without trouble. Hosts in VLAN 20 cannot reach
192.168.20.1 at all.

options.text: A subinterface number must match the VLAN ID before encapsulation takes effect.
The trunk to R1 needs switchport nonegotiate before subinterfaces will pass traffic.
Each subinterface needs its own no shutdown command before it will forward.
The second subinterface tags for VLAN 30, which the trunk does not carry.

items.explanation: The VLAN a subinterface serves is set by the encapsulation dot1Q value, not by the subinterface number, and the second one reads 30 while the trunk carries only VLANs 10 and 20, so nothing tagged for VLAN 20 ever reaches a matching subinterface. Option A inverts that relationship: the number is a label and is conventionally matched for readability alone. Option B names a command affecting trunk negotiation rather than tagging. Option C is wrong because subinterfaces follow the state of the physical interface, which is already up.

Option A is a real command, but it applies to a device with IP routing disabled, such as a Layer 2 switch, and is ignored on a routing router. Option B pairs the all-zeros network with a host mask, matching only the address 0.0.0.0. Option D marks a classful network as a candidate default and does not create this route.

Option A names 0.0.0.0 as a next hop, which does not identify the discard interface. Option B borrows the blackhole keyword used by other vendors; IOS does not accept it. Option C removes a route that was never configured, leaving the default to keep carrying the traffic to the ISP, which is the behaviour being eliminated.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The route was meant to cover only 192.168.16.0/24, but the mask was mistyped. What is the effect of the command as entered?

exhibit.content:
! R16 - relevant configuration
!
ip route 192.168.16.0 255.255.240.0 10.1.1.2
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
!

Traffic for every 192.168.x.x destination other than 192.168.16.0/24 is
expected to leave by the default route.

options.text: It covers only 192.168.16.0 through 192.168.16.255, exactly as intended.
It also captures 192.168.17.0 through 192.168.31.255, bypassing the default.
It is rejected at entry, because the address and mask are inconsistent.
It covers the whole of 192.168.0.0 through 192.168.255.255, capturing every private prefix.

items.explanation: 255.255.240.0 is a /20, and a /20 anchored at 192.168.16.0 spans sixteen values in the third octet, 16 through 31. Traffic to any of those now follows 10.1.1.2 rather than the default. Option A describes the /24 that was intended but not the mask that was typed. Option C expects a rejection, but 16 is a valid multiple of 16 so the pair is consistent and IOS accepts it silently, which is what makes the error hard to spot. Option D describes a /16, two steps broader than the mask shown.

Option A is ruled out by the S code, which marks a static route rather than a learned one. Option B repeats the frequent belief that this display form implies distance 0; the route still carries the static default of 1. Option C describes what happens on a multi-access link, but a point-to-point serial interface has one possible receiver and uses no ARP.

Option B is a static route but a /16 network route covering 65,534 addresses. Option C is the trap: it is a /32, but its code is L, meaning IOS created it automatically for the router's own interface address rather than an administrator configuring it. Option D is a static /20 network route, broader still than option B.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. No router ID has been set under the OSPF process. Which value does R1 adopt as its router ID when OSPF starts?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface Loopback0
 ip address 1.1.1.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
 ip address 9.9.9.9 255.255.255.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

items.explanation: With no router-id command, OSPF prefers the highest IPv4 address on any active loopback, and 9.9.9.9 outranks 1.1.1.1. Option A assumes Loopback0 wins because of its interface number, but the comparison is on address value, not interface order. Option B is the highest physical interface address, which is consulted only when no loopback exists. Option D would mean OSPF failed to pick an ID, in which case the process refuses to start rather than running with zeros.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. An engineer sets a router ID on R2, but the verification command still reports the old value. Which action makes the configured value take effect?

exhibit.content:
R2# show ip ospf | include Routing Process
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.1.2.1
R2#
R2# configure terminal
Enter configuration commands, one per line.  End with CNTL/Z.
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
% OSPF: Reload or use "clear ip ospf process" command, for this to take effect
R2(config-router)# end
R2#
R2# show ip ospf | include Routing Process
 Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 10.1.2.1

options.text: Clear the OSPF process with clear ip ospf process, or reload the router.
Re-enter the router-id command from interface configuration mode instead.
Remove and re-add the network statement so OSPF re-reads its configuration.
Configure a loopback with address 2.2.2.2 so the ID is derived from it.

items.explanation: A router ID is chosen when the OSPF process starts and is then held for the life of that process, which is why IOS prints the reload-or-clear notice visible in the exhibit. Option B invents an interface-level version of the command, which does not exist; router-id is a router-configuration command. Option C touches the network statement, which changes which interfaces run OSPF but never re-runs ID selection. Option D would matter only if no ID had been configured at all, and it still would not apply without restarting the process.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 and R2 are cabled together on the 10.1.1.0/30 link, both interfaces are up, but neither lists the other as a neighbour. Which difference in the output prevents the adjacency?

exhibit.content:
R1# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.1.1/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1

  No backup designated router on this network

  Neighbor Count is 0, Adjacent neighbor count is 0
----------------------------------------------------------
R2# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.1.2/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 2.2.2.2, Interface address 10.1.1.2
  No backup designated router on this network
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 5, Dead 20, Wait 20, Retransmit 5
  Neighbor Count is 0, Adjacent neighbor count is 0

options.text: Both routers report State DR, so neither will accept the other as a peer.
The hello and dead intervals differ between the two interfaces.
The two routers have different router IDs on the same segment.
The interface cost of 1 is too low for a broadcast network type.

items.explanation: Hello and dead intervals must match for two OSPF routers to become neighbours; R1 uses 10 and 40 while R2 uses 5 and 20, so the hellos are discarded and no adjacency forms. Option A misreads the symptom for the cause: both claim DR precisely because neither has seen the other, so it is a consequence. Option C inverts a requirement, since router IDs must be different rather than equal. Option D invents a minimum cost, and cost never affects whether an adjacency forms.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The link between R1 and R2 is up and both routers run OSPF in area 0, yet no adjacency forms. What prevents it?

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.5 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 2
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.1.1.4 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

options.text: The two routers have conflicting router IDs on the shared segment.
The OSPF process IDs differ, and they must match for an adjacency to form.
The hello intervals differ because only one router sets them explicitly.
The two interfaces do not sit in the same IPv4 subnet.

items.explanation: With a /30 mask, 10.1.1.1 belongs to 10.1.1.0/30 while 10.1.1.5 belongs to 10.1.1.4/30, so the addresses look adjacent but the interfaces are on different subnets and OSPF will not peer across them. Option B names the process IDs 1 and 2, which is the most tempting distractor here: the process ID is locally significant and need not match. Option A is wrong because 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 differ, which is what OSPF requires. Option C invents a timer difference neither configuration shows.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which router is elected designated router on the shared segment?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24  (broadcast segment)
      +---------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
                |               |               |               |
            +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+
            |  R1   |       |  R2   |       |  R3   |       |  R4   |
            +-------+       +-------+       +-------+       +-------+
        router-id 1.1.1.1   4.4.4.4         3.3.3.3         2.2.2.2
        ip ospf priority 1  priority 1      priority 5      priority 0

All four routers are powered on at the same moment and no adjacency
has formed yet.

options.text: R1
R2
R3
R4

items.explanation: DR election compares interface priority first and only falls back to the highest router ID on a tie. R3 carries priority 5, above every other router, so it becomes DR regardless of its router ID. Option B is the trap: R2 holds the highest router ID at 4.4.4.4 and would win only if all priorities were equal. Option A has neither the highest priority nor the highest ID. Option D is configured with priority 0, which bars it from becoming DR or BDR at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R5 joins a segment where the DR and BDR were elected hours earlier. What happens to the designated router role?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24  (broadcast segment)
      +---------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
                |               |               |               |
            +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+       +---+---+
            |  R1   |       |  R2   |       |  R3   |       |  R5   |
            +-------+       +-------+       +-------+       +-------+
        router-id 1.1.1.1   4.4.4.4         3.3.3.3         5.5.5.5
        priority 1          priority 1      priority 5      priority 10

R3 was elected DR and R2 BDR some hours ago. R5 has just now been
cabled to the segment and brought up.

options.text: R3 stays designated router, because OSPF elections are not preemptive.
R5 becomes designated router at once, since its priority is the highest present.
R5 becomes backup designated router and is promoted at the next hello interval.
The election is rerun, making R5 designated router and R3 backup designated router.

items.explanation: OSPF elections are non-preemptive: once a DR and BDR are established, a newly arrived router with a better priority does not displace them, and R5 becomes a DROTHER until the DR fails. Option B applies the priority comparison that governs only a fresh election. Option C invents a promotion path through the BDR role, but the sitting BDR keeps its place too. Option D assumes any topology change reruns the election, which would cause exactly the churn that non-preemption exists to prevent.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R7 must be prevented from ever becoming the designated router or backup designated router on GigabitEthernet0/0, while continuing to run OSPF there. Which command accomplishes that?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ip ospf interface brief
Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C
Gi0/0        1     0               10.1.1.1/24        1     DR    3/3
Gi0/1        1     0               10.1.2.1/30        1     P2P   1/1

options.text: R7(config-router)# priority 0
R7(config-if)# ip ospf priority 0
R7(config-if)# ip ospf priority 255
R7(config-router)# passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: Priority is an interface setting, and the value 0 removes the router from the election while leaving OSPF running on the link. Option A has the right keyword and value but is entered in router configuration mode, where priority is not a valid command. Option C sets 255, the highest priority, which makes the router almost certain to become DR, the opposite of the requirement. Option D silences OSPF on the interface entirely, so no adjacency would form at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour reached over Serial0/0/0 shows FULL with no role after the slash. What does that indicate about the link?

exhibit.content:
R8# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:36    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0
3.3.3.3           1   FULL/DR         00:00:33    10.1.1.3        GigabitEthernet0/0
4.4.4.4           0   FULL/  -        00:00:38    10.2.2.2        Serial0/0/0

options.text: The neighbour has not finished exchanging its link-state database with R8.
The OSPF priority on that neighbour's interface has been set to zero.
The designated router for that segment has not been elected yet.
The link uses a point-to-point network type, which elects no DR or BDR.

items.explanation: OSPF elects a DR and BDR only on multi-access networks; on a point-to-point link there is no role to print, so the state shows FULL with a dash. Option A misreads FULL, which is the final state and confirms the databases are already synchronised. Option B is tempting because the Pri column reads 0, but that is what a point-to-point interface reports, not evidence of a configured priority. Option C would leave the neighbours in a transitional state rather than FULL.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which network statement enables OSPF on GigabitEthernet0/0 in area 0 without also enabling it on GigabitEthernet0/1?

exhibit.content:
! R9 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.1.1.65 255.255.255.192
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 9.9.9.9
!

OSPF must be enabled on GigabitEthernet0/0 in area 0, and on no other
interface.

options.text: network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 1

items.explanation: The network statement takes a wildcard mask, and a /30 corresponds to 0.0.0.3, which matches 10.1.1.0 through 10.1.1.3 and so covers GigabitEthernet0/0 alone. Option A supplies a subnet mask where the command expects a wildcard; IOS reads the value as a wildcard anyway, so the match bears no relation to the /30 link. Option B widens the match to 10.1.1.0 through 10.1.1.255, which also picks up 10.1.1.65 on GigabitEthernet0/1 and violates the requirement. Option D has the correct wildcard but places the interface in area 1, breaking the single-area design.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the effect of R10's configuration on the 10.1.1.0/30 link?

exhibit.content:
! R10 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 10.10.10.10
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!

A neighbouring router is correctly configured for area 0 on the far end
of the 10.1.1.0/30 link.

options.text: R10 advertises the 10.1.1.0/30 prefix into OSPF but forms no adjacency on that link.
R10 stops advertising 10.1.1.0/30 and forms no adjacency on that link.
R10 forms the adjacency normally but withholds the 10.1.1.0/30 prefix.
R10 is unaffected, because passive-interface applies only to distance-vector protocols.

items.explanation: A passive interface stops OSPF from sending or accepting hellos on that link, so no adjacency can form, while the network statement still causes the prefix to be advertised into the area. Option B misses that half: suppressing hellos does not withdraw the prefix. Option C reverses the behaviour entirely. Option D confuses OSPF with RIP or EIGRP, where the command exists as well; it is equally effective under OSPF, which is exactly why misapplying it silently breaks adjacencies.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which neighbour is acting as the designated router on GigabitEthernet0/0?

exhibit.content:
R11# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
5.5.5.5           1   FULL/DROTHER    00:00:31    10.1.1.5        GigabitEthernet0/0
6.6.6.6           2   FULL/DR         00:00:34    10.1.1.6        GigabitEthernet0/0
7.7.7.7           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:39    10.1.1.7        GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: The State column carries the neighbour's role after the slash, and 6.6.6.6 is the row that reads FULL/DR. Option A is the DROTHER row, a neighbour that took no role in the election. Option C is the BDR, which stands by rather than serving as DR. Option D quotes an address from the Address column instead of the Neighbor ID column, which is a different field entirely and belongs to the 5.5.5.5 row.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. R1 and R2 share an up/up link but never become neighbours. Which two configuration differences account for that? (Choose two.)

exhibit.content:
! R1 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 10
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
!
----------------------------------------------------------
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.252
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 1
!

options.text: The two routers have been given identical router IDs.
The two interfaces have been addressed in different subnets.
The interfaces have been placed in different OSPF areas.
The configured hello intervals do not match.
One of the two interfaces has been configured as passive.

items.explanation: Two routers must agree on the area and on their hello and dead timers before an adjacency will form; R1 uses area 0 with hello 10 while R2 uses area 1 with hello 5, so both checks fail. Option A is wrong because the IDs 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2 are properly distinct. Option B is wrong because 10.1.1.1 and 10.1.1.2 both sit inside 10.1.1.0/30. Option E describes a command that appears in neither configuration.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The adjacency between R13 and its neighbour never advances beyond the state shown. Which cause does the remaining output point to?

exhibit.content:
R13# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/DR      00:00:35    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0

R13# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
R13#
----------------------------------------------------------
R14# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0 | include MTU
  MTU 9000 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,

options.text: The interface MTU values on the two routers do not match.
The dead interval expired before the databases could be exchanged.
Both routers claim the designated router role for the segment.
The neighbour's router ID duplicates one already known to R13.

items.explanation: An adjacency that halts at EXSTART or EXCHANGE points at the database exchange itself, and the two interfaces report 1500 and 9000 bytes, so the routers cannot agree on a payload size and the exchange never completes. Option B is wrong because an expired dead interval drops the neighbour out of the table rather than freezing it in EXSTART. Option C describes a condition that resolves through election rather than stalling the exchange. Option D would prevent the neighbour from being listed at all rather than holding it mid-exchange.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The OSPF process on R14 carries no network statements, and the design calls for enabling OSPF directly on the interface instead. Which command does that?

exhibit.content:
! R14 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
!
router ospf 1
 router-id 14.14.14.14
!

options.text: R14(config-router)# network GigabitEthernet0/0 area 0
R14(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0
R14(config-if)# ospf 1 area 0
R14(config-router)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0 area 0

items.explanation: The interface-level form is ip ospf followed by the process ID and the area, entered under the interface, and it enables OSPF on that interface without any network statement. Option A keeps the network keyword, which expects an address and wildcard rather than an interface name. Option C drops the leading ip, so IOS does not recognise the command. Option D tries to nest an interface command inside router configuration mode, mixing the two modes that the interface-level form exists to separate.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What OSPF cost does R15 assign to Serial0/0/0?

exhibit.content:
R15# show interfaces Serial0/0/0 | include BW
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1544 Kbit/sec, DLY 20000 usec,
R15#
R15# show ip ospf | include Reference bandwidth
 Reference bandwidth unit is 100 mbps

items.explanation: Cost is the reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, so 100,000,000 divided by 1,544,000 gives 64.77, and OSPF discards the remainder to leave 64. Option C rounds the quotient up to 65 instead of truncating, which is the single commonest arithmetic slip on this calculation. Option A is the cost a link at or above the reference bandwidth receives, since the formula floors at 1. Option B quotes the reference bandwidth itself rather than the result of the division.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. From which neighbour has R16 most recently received OSPF routing information?

*** IP Routing is NSF aware ***

Routing Protocol is "ospf 1"
  Outgoing update filter list for all interfaces is not set
  Incoming update filter list for all interfaces is not set
  Router ID 16.16.16.16
  Number of areas in this router is 1. 1 normal 0 stub 0 nssa
  Maximum path: 4

    10.1.1.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

Option B reads the larger elapsed time as the more recent, inverting the column's meaning. Option C quotes R16's own router ID, which identifies the local router rather than a source. Option D takes a value from the Routing for Networks list, which records what R16 advertises, not who it hears from.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour has been sitting in the state shown for several minutes. What does that state indicate?

exhibit.content:
R17# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   INIT/DROTHER    00:00:31    10.1.1.2        GigabitEthernet0/0

options.text: The neighbour finished exchanging databases but has not installed the routes.
R17 has seen the neighbour's hello, but the neighbour has not yet seen R17's.
The two routers disagree over which of them is the designated router.
The dead interval has expired and the neighbour is being removed from the table.

items.explanation: INIT means hellos are arriving in one direction only: R17 has heard the neighbour, but has not yet seen its own router ID listed in the neighbour's hello, so the relationship cannot advance to two-way. It usually points at something filtering traffic in one direction. Option A describes FULL, the state that follows a completed exchange. Option C describes an election dispute, which does not hold a neighbour at INIT. Option D is contradicted by the Dead Time of 31 seconds still counting down.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which OSPF cost does R18 apply to traffic leaving Serial0/0/0?

Interface    PID   Area            IP Address/Mask    Cost  State Nbrs F/C

items.explanation: The Cost column on the Serial0/0/0 row reads 64, which is the value OSPF adds when a path leaves by that interface. Option A takes the cost from the GigabitEthernet0/0 row, reading the right column on the wrong line. Option B quotes 110, which is OSPF's administrative distance and never appears in this output at all. Option D assumes an unlisted interface costs nothing, but every OSPF-enabled interface carries a cost of at least 1.

Both routers place the interface in area 0 and use default timers.

options.text: A designated router and backup are still elected, but the hello timers halve.
No adjacency forms, because Ethernet interfaces cannot use that network type.
The adjacency reaches FULL, but no link-state advertisements cross the link.
No designated router is elected, and the state shows FULL with no role.

items.explanation: Changing the network type to point-to-point tells OSPF to treat the segment as having exactly two routers, so the election is skipped entirely and the neighbour prints as FULL with a dash where a role would otherwise appear. Option A keeps an election that the network type removes. Option B assumes the type is tied to the physical medium, but it is a software setting commonly applied to Ethernet links carrying only two routers. Option C would leave the routers with no shared topology, which FULL rules out.

Option A confuses the wildcard, which selects which interfaces participate, with the length that gets advertised. Option B describes summarisation to a classful boundary, which would produce a shorter prefix rather than a longer one. Option D invokes an area difference that the single-area configuration rules out.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which address should hosts on the 10.1.1.0/24 segment carry as their default gateway?

exhibit.content:

                     P indicates configured to preempt.

Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       1    110 P Active  local           10.1.1.3        10.1.1.1

items.explanation: Hosts point at the virtual address the group presents, listed in the Virtual IP column as 10.1.1.1, which survives a failover because the standby router adopts it. Option A is R1's own interface address, and pointing hosts there would strand them the moment R1 failed, which is the entire problem an FHRP exists to solve. Option B is the standby router's real address and has the same weakness. Option D reads the Pri column value of 110 as though it were part of an address.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which virtual MAC address does R2 use for this HSRP group?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 1
 standby 10 ip 10.1.1.1
 standby 10 priority 110
 standby 10 preempt
!

items.explanation: An HSRP version 1 virtual MAC is 0000.0C07.AC followed by the group number in hexadecimal, and group 10 in hex is 0a, giving 0000.0c07.ac0a. Option A writes the group as the literal digits 10, producing 0000.0c07.ac10, which is a genuine virtual MAC but belongs to group 16. Option C uses the 0000.5E00.01 range, which identifies VRRP rather than HSRP. Option D is the group 1 address, ignoring the configured group number entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which role does each router hold once R1 has recovered?

exhibit.content:
10.1.1.0/24

                |                   |
            +---+---+           +---+---+
            |  R1   |           |  R2   |

          10.1.1.2            10.1.1.3
          priority 110        priority 100
          no preempt          no preempt

Virtual IP 10.1.1.1, HSRP group 1 on both routers.

R1 was active. Its uplink failed, R2 took over, and R1 has now
recovered and re-formed its HSRP relationship with R2.

options.text: R2 stays active and R1 becomes standby, despite R1's higher priority.
R1 resumes the active role at once, because its priority is the higher of the two.
Both routers hold the active role until the next hello exchange separates them.
R1 stays out of the group until preemption is configured on R2.

items.explanation: Priority decides an election, but without the preempt keyword a returning router cannot displace a sitting active router, so R2 keeps the role and R1 settles for standby. Option B applies the priority comparison to a group that has already elected, which is what preemption exists to enable and neither router has it. Option C describes a split-active state that the hello exchange prevents. Option D inverts the requirement: preemption would be needed on R1, the router trying to take over, not on R2.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What does PC1 experience after R1 loses power?

options.text: PC1 must be reconfigured with R2's interface address as its gateway.
PC1 has to renew its DHCP lease to be issued a new default gateway.
PC1 loses reachability until its ARP cache expires and it re-resolves.
PC1 keeps the same gateway, as R2 takes over the virtual IP and MAC.

items.explanation: The standby router assumes both the virtual IP address and the virtual MAC address, so the entry already cached by PC1 stays valid and forwarding resumes without any change on the host. That property is the whole purpose of a first hop redundancy protocol. Option A would require touching every host, which is precisely what the protocol avoids. Option B assumes a DHCP dependency PC1 does not have, since its gateway is static. Option C is the most tempting error: it would be true if only the IP moved, but the virtual MAC moves with it.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Once both routers have finished negotiating, which one forwards traffic sent to 10.1.1.1?

exhibit.content:

            +---+---+           +---+---+
            |  R1   |           |  R2   |
            +-------+           +-------+
          10.1.1.2            10.1.1.3
          standby 1 priority 90    standby 1 priority 120
          standby 1 preempt        standby 1 preempt

Both routers use virtual IP 10.1.1.1 in HSRP group 1 and are
brought up at the same time.

options.text: R1, because it holds the lower interface address on the segment.
Both routers share the load, since each is configured to preempt.
R2, because its configured priority is the higher of the two.
Whichever router completed boot first and claimed the virtual address.

items.explanation: HSRP elects the router with the numerically higher priority, so R2's 120 beats R1's 90 and R2 becomes active while R1 stands by. Option A applies a lowest-address tie-break, which HSRP consults only when priorities are equal, and even then it prefers the higher address. Option B assumes load sharing between the two, but a single HSRP group has exactly one forwarder. Option D describes what would happen without preemption, yet both routers carry the preempt keyword, so the higher priority asserts itself regardless of boot order.

options.text: R6's priority falls to 90, and the router at 10.1.1.3 preempts to become active.
R6's priority falls to 90, but R6 stays active because it already owns the role.
R6 leaves the group entirely and stops responding to the virtual IP address.
R6's priority is unaffected, since tracking influences only the routing table.

items.explanation: The tracking statement decrements R6's priority by 20 when the object goes down, taking 110 to 90, which is below the standby router's 100; because both routers are configured to preempt, the router at 10.1.1.3 then takes the active role. Option B ignores preemption, which is exactly what makes the decrement useful. Option C overstates the effect, as a lowered priority demotes the router rather than removing it. items.explanation: An ARP request for the virtual IP is answered with the group's virtual MAC, 0000.0c07.ac01, which is why the cached entry stays correct after a failover moves the role to the other router. options.text: The routers negotiate a single group and elect R1 as the active router.
Each router becomes the active router for its own group.
Both routers answer ARP for 10.1.1.1 with different virtual MACs.
Neither router responds to traffic addressed to 10.1.1.1.
R1 suppresses R2's group because it holds the higher configured priority.

items.explanation: HSRP routers only negotiate with peers in the same group number, so R1 in group 1 and R2 in group 2 never see each other; each declares itself active for its own group, and each answers for 10.1.1.1 with the virtual MAC derived from its own group number. Option A assumes the shared virtual IP is enough to pair them, when the group number is what binds peers. Option D contradicts both routers being active. Option E applies a priority comparison across groups that never communicate.
